element_a.enriched_title: Pronoun and occupation co-occurrence counts in ELMo training corpus
element_a.enriched_content: Aggregate frequency statistics are reported for male (M) and female (F) pronouns in the ELMo training corpus, alongside how often each pronoun co-occurs with stereotypically male-biased versus female-biased occupation terms. The comparisons characterize gender imbalance both in overall entity mention rates (M vs F pronoun totals) and in association patterns between pronouns and occupation stereotypes (M pronouns with M-biased jobs, F pronouns with F-biased jobs). These corpus-level co-occurrence asymmetries motivate later claims that contextual embeddings can encode and propagate gender information unequally across male and female entities.

element_a.enriched_content: This equation defines the false-positive cost associated with the optimal time-indexed predictor by combining two summary statistics of its outputs under the distribution G_t. The first expectation measures the average score/prediction h_t(x), while the second expectation measures the average squared score, acting like a correction based on the output’s second moment (e.g., reflecting confidence or variability). The difference between these two moments is then rescaled by 1/(1−mu_t), which typically normalizes by the mass of the negative class so the quantity corresponds to false positives among negatives. In the paper’s method, this provides a computable expression for c_fp(h_t^*) from distributional expectations, enabling comparison or optimization alongside the corresponding false-negative term.

element_a.enriched_content: The formula computes the generalized false-positive rate for a perfectly calibrated classifier within group G_t. It takes the difference between the group-average prediction E[h_t(x)] and the group-average squared prediction E[h_t(x)^2], which captures how much probability mass the classifier assigns without being overly concentrated near 0 or 1. node_group.enriched_title: False-positive cost for the optimal predictor at time t

variables.c_fp(h_t^*): false-positive cost (or rate/cost surrogate) achieved by the optimal rule at time t
variables.h_t^*: optimal predictor/decision function at time t
variables.h_t(x): model output or score produced by the predictor on input x

variables.G_t: data-generating distribution at time t over which expectations are taken

node_group.enriched_content: This equation defines the false-positive cost associated with the optimal time-indexed predictor by combining two summary statistics of its outputs under the distribution G_t. The first expectation measures the average score/prediction h_t(x), while the second expectation measures the average squared score, acting like a correction based on the output’s second moment (e.g., reflecting confidence or variability). The difference between these two moments is then rescaled by 1/(1−mu_t), which typically normalizes by the mass of the negative class so the quantity corresponds to false positives among negatives. In the paper’s method, this provides a computable expression for c_fp(h_t^*) from distributional expectations, enabling comparison or optimization alongside the corresponding false-negative term.

element_a.enriched_content: The formula computes the generalized false-positive rate for a perfectly calibrated classifier within group G_t. It takes the difference between the group-average prediction E[h_t(x)] and the group-average squared prediction E[h_t(x)^2], which captures how much probability mass the classifier assigns without being overly concentrated near 0 or 1. element_b.enriched_content: This identity rewrites a centered sum of squares—total energy in the values minus the squared mean term—into an equivalent average of all pairwise squared differences among the z_i. The left-hand side computes dispersion by subtracting (1/k) times the squared sum (a mean-correction) from the sum of individual squares. The right-hand side shows the same dispersion as the average pairwise disagreement, which is useful in methods that switch between variance/centering formulations and pairwise-distance (scatter) formulations for analysis or optimization.

element_b.enriched_title: Stereotypical analogies versus generated analogies under debiasing methods

enriched_metadata.axes: x-axis: number of generated analogies; y-axis: number of stereotypic analogies

element_b.enriched_content: As the number of generated analogies increases (0–160), the count of stereotypic analogies rises for the original embedding (“before”) from ~0 up to about 29. Soft-debiased embeddings reduce this growth modestly, ending around ~25 stereotypic analogies at the highest generation counts, with a similar upward trend after ~70–80 analogies. Hard-debiased embeddings suppress stereotypic analogies much more strongly, staying near 0 until roughly ~60 analogies and remaining below ~10 even at ~150 generated analogies. Overall, hard debiasing produces the largest reduction in stereotypical analogies relative to both the baseline and soft debiasing.

element_b.enriched_content: The equation specifies a two-step generative process: first draw a latent representation z from a chosen prior, then generate an observed sample x from a model distribution conditioned on both z and an additional variable s. In the paper’s method, this expresses the decoder/generative component used to model data while explicitly accounting for (or aiming to control invariance to) the influence of s.

element_b.enriched_title: Linear privacy-accuracy degradation as a function of epsilon

variables.PAD(ε): privacy-accuracy degradation score (or penalty metric) evaluated at ε
variables.ε: privacy/leakage parameter controlling how much information can be inferred

element_b.enriched_content: The equation defines a simple metric PAD(ε) that quantifies how privacy/attribute leakage changes with the leakage parameter ε. It is linear in ε: the constant factor 2 sets the scale, while the term (1 − 2ε) decreases the score as ε increases, reflecting worse privacy (or weaker protection) with higher leakage. In the surrounding discussion about penalties being satisfied even when probabilistic predictions still leak information, this metric provides a direct way to relate allowable inference strength (ε) to the paper’s privacy-aware representation learning objectives in domain adaptation.

node_group.enriched_title: Linear privacy-accuracy degradation as a function of epsilon

node_group.enriched_content: The equation defines a simple metric PAD(ε) that quantifies how privacy/attribute leakage changes with the leakage parameter ε. It is linear in ε: the constant factor 2 sets the scale, while the term (1 − 2ε) decreases the score as ε increases, reflecting worse privacy (or weaker protection) with higher leakage. In the surrounding discussion about penalties being satisfied even when probabilistic predictions still leak information, this metric provides a direct way to relate allowable inference strength (ε) to the paper’s privacy-aware representation learning objectives in domain adaptation.

element_a.enriched_content: Eight density subplots compare original predictions to counterfactual predictions after swapping a protected attribute (black↔white, asian↔white, mexican↔white, female↔male), with results shown for a “Full” model (top row) versus an “Unaware” model (bottom row). element_b.enriched_content: As the number of generated analogies increases (0–160), the count of stereotypic analogies rises for the original embedding (“before”) from ~0 up to about 29. element_b.enriched_title: Racial differences in COMPAS decile score distributions

enriched_metadata.axes: x-axis: COMPAS decile score (1–10); y-axis: frequency (proportion of defendants in each decile)

element_b.enriched_content: Relative frequency bars by COMPAS decile indicate White defendants are concentrated in low scores, especially decile 1 (~0.29) and decile 2 (~0.15), with steadily decreasing mass toward higher deciles. Black defendants have a flatter distribution with much less mass at decile 1 (~0.11) and comparatively higher frequencies in mid-to-high deciles (roughly ~0.09–0.11 from deciles 4–9). Above decile 6, Black frequencies generally exceed White frequencies, while the reverse holds for deciles 1–4. The overall pattern implies higher assigned risk scores for Black defendants on average and more low-risk assignments for White defendants.

element_b.enriched_title: Causal mediation graph with unobserved confounding blocking natural direct effect
element_b.enriched_content: A directed acyclic graph contains observed nodes C, A, M, and Y (black) plus an unobserved node U (gray). Red arrows U→M and U→Y add unmeasured confounding between the mediator and outcome, creating a backdoor path M←U→Y that prevents identification of the natural direct effect despite the observed adjustments.

variables.PAD(ε): privacy-accuracy degradation score (or penalty metric) evaluated at ε

element_b.enriched_content: The equation defines a simple metric PAD(ε) that quantifies how privacy/attribute leakage changes with the leakage parameter ε. It is linear in ε: the constant factor 2 sets the scale, while the term (1 − 2ε) decreases the score as ε increases, reflecting worse privacy (or weaker protection) with higher leakage. In the surrounding discussion about penalties being satisfied even when probabilistic predictions still leak information, this metric provides a direct way to relate allowable inference strength (ε) to the paper’s privacy-aware representation learning objectives in domain adaptation.

element_a.enriched_title: Linear structural equations for a causal mediation model

variables.C: exogenous covariate/background factor with noise epsilon_c
variables.M: mediator variable affected by A and C plus noise
variables.L: intermediate outcome/mediator affected by A, C, and M plus noise
variables.Y: final outcome affected by A, C, M, and L plus noise
variables.theta: model coefficients for intercepts and causal links
variables.epsilon_*: independent disturbance (unobserved) terms for each equation

element_a.enriched_content: The equation block defines a generative causal model where the treatment A is Bernoulli with probability pi, and the other variables are produced by linear structural equations with additive noise. M, L, and Y each combine an intercept term with contributions from upstream variables (A and C, plus M into L, and M and L into Y), with theta parameters encoding the strength of each causal link. This parameterization supports the paper’s counterfactual mediation analysis by providing an explicit SCM in which direct and indirect paths from A to Y (through M and through M then L) can be computed via interventions.

variables.L: intermediate outcome/mediator affected by A, C, and M plus noise

element_a.enriched_content: The equation block defines a generative causal model where the treatment A is Bernoulli with probability pi, and the other variables are produced by linear structural equations with additive noise. M, L, and Y each combine an intercept term with contributions from upstream variables (A and C, plus M into L, and M and L into Y), with theta parameters encoding the strength of each causal link. This parameterization supports the paper’s counterfactual mediation analysis by providing an explicit SCM in which direct and indirect paths from A to Y (through M and through M then L) can be computed via interventions.

element_a.enriched_title: G-computation integral for outcome distribution under mediated intervention

variables.Y: outcome variable whose distribution is being computed
variables.a: treatment/exposure level used in some conditional models
variables.a': reference/counterfactual treatment level used for L model
variables.C: baseline covariates/confounders to be integrated out
variables.M: mediator variable generated under treatment a
variables.L: intermediate variable (post-treatment covariate) generated under a'

element_a.enriched_content: This expression computes a marginal (interventional/counterfactual) distribution of the outcome Y by integrating over covariates C, mediator M, and intermediate variable L. The term p(Y|a,C,M,L) models the outcome given treatment and upstream variables, while p(L|a',C,M) and p(M|a,C) specify how L and M are generated under different treatment levels (a' for L, a for M), with p(C) providing the baseline distribution of confounders. Together, these factors form a g-computation formula used to identify a path-specific or mediated effect by stitching together conditional models and then marginalizing over unobserved/latent components along the causal graph.

node_group.enriched_title: Racial differences in COMPAS decile score distributions

enriched_metadata.axes: x-axis: COMPAS decile score (1–10); y-axis: frequency (proportion of defendants in each decile)

node_group.enriched_content: Relative frequency bars by COMPAS decile indicate White defendants are concentrated in low scores, especially decile 1 (~0.29) and decile 2 (~0.15), with steadily decreasing mass toward higher deciles. Black defendants have a flatter distribution with much less mass at decile 1 (~0.11) and comparatively higher frequencies in mid-to-high deciles (roughly ~0.09–0.11 from deciles 4–9). Above decile 6, Black frequencies generally exceed White frequencies, while the reverse holds for deciles 1–4. The overall pattern implies higher assigned risk scores for Black defendants on average and more low-risk assignments for White defendants.

element_b.enriched_title: Observed recidivism increases with COMPAS decile for Black and White groups

enriched_metadata.axes: X-axis: COMPAS decile score (1–10). Y-axis: observed probability of recidivism (0–1).

element_b.enriched_content: Grouped bars report observed recidivism probability by COMPAS decile for Black (gray) and White (orange) defendants, with 95% confidence-interval error bars. Recidivism rises roughly monotonically with score for both groups, from about 0.2–0.3 at deciles 1–2 to about 0.7–0.85 by deciles 8–10. Within most deciles the Black and White rates are close and their confidence intervals substantially overlap, with Black slightly higher in several bins (e.g., around decile 10: ~0.85 Black vs ~0.70 White). Overall, the pattern indicates similar conditional recidivism rates across races at a given COMPAS score, consistent with approximate calibration/test fairness.

element_b.enriched_title: Accuracy–fairness efficient frontier curves for sentencing regression models

enriched_metadata.axes: x-axis: Fairness Loss (0 to ~0.07); y-axis: Mean Squared Error (MSE, ~0.90 to ~1.02).

element_b.enriched_content: Four efficient-frontier curves trace the tradeoff between minimizing fairness loss and minimizing prediction error (MSE). As fairness loss increases from 0 toward ~0.07, MSE decreases from about 1.0 down to roughly 0.905–0.91, with the steepest improvement occurring at very small fairness loss. The group-based approaches cluster near very low fairness loss (≈0–0.01) with MSE around 0.91–0.92, while the individual-fairness curves extend across the full fairness-loss range and generally achieve slightly lower MSE at moderate-to-high fairness loss. Overall, relaxing fairness constraints yields diminishing returns in MSE reduction after about 0.03–0.05 fairness loss.

variables.z_i: scalar value for index i (e.g., sample/feature/component)

element_b.enriched_content: This identity rewrites a centered sum of squares—total energy in the values minus the squared mean term—into an equivalent average of all pairwise squared differences among the z_i. The left-hand side computes dispersion by subtracting (1/k) times the squared sum (a mean-correction) from the sum of individual squares. The right-hand side shows the same dispersion as the average pairwise disagreement, which is useful in methods that switch between variance/centering formulations and pairwise-distance (scatter) formulations for analysis or optimization.

element_a.enriched_content: This formula computes the marginal distribution of the potential (interventional) outcome Y_a by averaging the conditional outcome distribution over the population distribution of covariates C. element_b.caption: Figure 1: Five example images from the imSitu visual semantic role labeling (vSRL) dataset. Each image is paired with a table describing a situation: the verb, cooking, its semantic roles, i.e agent, and noun values filling that role, i.e. woman. In the imSitu training set, $33 \%$ of cooking images have man in the agent role while the rest have woman. After training a Conditional Random Field (CRF), bias is amplified: man fills $16 \%$ of agent roles in cooking images. To reduce this bias amplification our calibration method adjusts weights of CRF potentials associated with biased predictions. After applying our methods, man appears in the agent role of $20 \%$ of cooking images, reducing the bias amplification by $2 5 \%$ , while keeping the CRF vSRL performance unchanged.

element_b.enriched_content: Three systems (STAT in blue circles, RULE in green triangles, NEURAL in red pentagons) plot occupation points against text-derived % female, with fitted trend lines and confidence bands. As the % female in text increases, all systems shift toward more female-pronoun linking (positive y), but RULE exhibits the steepest slope, reaching near +100 around 80–90% female, while STAT rises more moderately and NEURAL increases only slightly. Many occupations at low x cluster near strong male preference (around −100 to −50), and a dashed horizontal line at y=0 marks parity, which the systems cross at different x ranges (RULE earlier, STAT around mid-range, NEURAL later). The overall pattern indicates that system decisions not only track occupational gender prevalence but can amplify it, especially for the rule-based system.

element_b.enriched_content: This identity rewrites a centered sum of squares—total energy in the values minus the squared mean term—into an equivalent average of all pairwise squared differences among the z_i. The left-hand side computes dispersion by subtracting (1/k) times the squared sum (a mean-correction) from the sum of individual squares. The right-hand side shows the same dispersion as the average pairwise disagreement, which is useful in methods that switch between variance/centering formulations and pairwise-distance (scatter) formulations for analysis or optimization.

element_b.caption: Figure 1: Five example images from the imSitu visual semantic role labeling (vSRL) dataset. Each image is paired with a table describing a situation: the verb, cooking, its semantic roles, i.e agent, and noun values filling that role, i.e. woman. In the imSitu training set, $33 \%$ of cooking images have man in the agent role while the rest have woman. After training a Conditional Random Field (CRF), bias is amplified: man fills $16 \%$ of agent roles in cooking images. To reduce this bias amplification our calibration method adjusts weights of CRF potentials associated with biased predictions. After applying our methods, man appears in the agent role of $20 \%$ of cooking images, reducing the bias amplification by $2 5 \%$ , while keeping the CRF vSRL performance unchanged.

element_b.enriched_title: Coreference gender preference correlates with occupation’s female prevalence in text

enriched_metadata.axes: x-axis: % female by occupation in text (Bergsma and Lin, 2006); y-axis: gendered pronoun resolution by occupations (%Female − %Male).

element_b.enriched_content: Three systems (STAT in blue circles, RULE in green triangles, NEURAL in red pentagons) plot occupation points against text-derived % female, with fitted trend lines and confidence bands. As the % female in text increases, all systems shift toward more female-pronoun linking (positive y), but RULE exhibits the steepest slope, reaching near +100 around 80–90% female, while STAT rises more moderately and NEURAL increases only slightly. Many occupations at low x cluster near strong male preference (around −100 to −50), and a dashed horizontal line at y=0 marks parity, which the systems cross at different x ranges (RULE earlier, STAT around mid-range, NEURAL later). The overall pattern indicates that system decisions not only track occupational gender prevalence but can amplify it, especially for the rule-based system.

element_a.enriched_content: This equation defines a path-specific causal effect that isolates the contribution of particular causal routes from treatment A to outcome Y, especially those passing through the mediator M. element_a.enriched_content: This equation defines a path-specific causal effect that isolates the contribution of particular causal routes from treatment A to outcome Y, especially those passing through the mediator M. The first expectation is the mean outcome under a mixed (nested) counterfactual where A is set to a, the mediator is allowed to take its treatment-induced value M_a, but other pathway variables L are forced to behave as they would under the baseline \bar{a}. Subtracting the mean baseline outcome \langle Y_{\bar{a}} \rangle removes the overall reference level, leaving only the average effect attributable to the selected pathways. In the paper’s causal Bayesian network framework, this quantity operationalizes “effect of treatment” when only specific direct/indirect paths (e.g., through M) are considered relevant.

element_a.enriched_title: Sex-stratified income prediction error rates under adversarial debiasing
element_a.enriched_content: False positive rate (FPR) and false negative rate (FNR) for income-bracket classification are reported separately for Male and Female subgroups under two training regimes: standard training and adversarial debiasing. element_b.enriched_title: Projected adversarial-gradient update direction for predictor weights

variables.∇_W L_P: gradient of predictor loss w.r.t. W
variables.∇_W L_A: gradient of adversary loss w.r.t. W
variables.proj_{∇_W L_A}(∇_W L_P): component of the predictor gradient aligned with the adversary gradient direction
variables.α: scalar weight controlling strength of adversarial term

element_b.enriched_content: The expression defines a composite update direction for the predictor parameters that balances improving the predictor task while resisting an adversary. It starts from the predictor loss gradient, subtracts its projection onto the adversary-loss gradient so the predictor does not move in a direction that would help the adversary, and then subtracts an additional scaled adversary-gradient term to actively increase the adversary’s loss. In the method, this yields an update that preserves task learning while discouraging representations that the adversary can exploit.

element_a.enriched_title: Stability declines with increasing regularization across three methods

enriched_metadata.axes: x-axis: regularization parameter λ (0 to 0.05); y-axis: stability metric stab (≈30 to 100)

element_a.enriched_content: At λ=0, KAAS-St starts highest (near 100) while ZVRG-St and GYR-St begin lower (around the 70–75 range). All three methods drop sharply by λ≈0.01 to around the high-30s/low-40s, with ZVRG-St and GYR-St remaining close to each other thereafter. KAAS-St stays consistently above the other two for λ>0, dipping to roughly 40–45 near λ≈0.02 and then fluctuating around 50–58, while ZVRG-St and GYR-St gradually drift down to the mid-30s by λ=0.05.

element_b.content: $$\operatorname {I} \left[ \mathcal {A} _ {S} (x) \geq 0 \right] = \operatorname {I} \left[ \mathcal {A} _ {S ^ {i}} (x) \geq 0 \right].$$
element_b.enriched_title: Indicator equality enforcing stable sign of scoring function

variables.\\operatorname{I}[\\cdot]: indicator function returning 1 if the condition holds and 0 otherwise
variables.\\mathcal{A}_S(x): real-valued scoring/aggregation function computed using set S, evaluated at input x
variables.\\mathcal{A}_{S^i}(x): corresponding scoring/aggregation function computed using an alternative set S^i
variables.S: reference sample set or subset used to build the score function
variables.S^i: modified/alternative sample set (e.g., with the i-th element changed or removed)
variables.x: input instance at which the score is evaluated

element_b.enriched_content: The equation states that the binary decision obtained by thresholding the score at zero is identical whether the score is computed from set S or from an alternative set S^i. The indicator function converts the real-valued score into a 0/1 outcome, so the equality enforces invariance of the sign (and hence the predicted label/decision) under the change from S to S^i. In a paper’s method, such a condition typically formalizes a stability or robustness property: small perturbations to the data set do not flip the model’s decision on x.

element_a.enriched_content: Two stacked panels compare multiple colored point estimates with horizontal uncertainty bars for average odds difference, with most methods producing negative values between about −0.22 and 0.00. Points associated with disparate impact removal cluster around roughly −0.20 with performance near 0.74–0.75, indicating persistent negative average odds differences despite similar performance. Calibrated equal-odds postprocessing includes points much closer to 0 (around −0.02 to +0.10) while maintaining performance in the ~0.70–0.76 range, suggesting improved parity with modest performance variation. A notable outlier appears near −0.10 average odds difference with lower performance around 0.66, highlighting a potential fairness–performance trade-off for at least one setting.

element_b.enriched_content: This identity rewrites a centered sum of squares—total energy in the values minus the squared mean term—into an equivalent average of all pairwise squared differences among the z_i. The left-hand side computes dispersion by subtracting (1/k) times the squared sum (a mean-correction) from the sum of individual squares. element_b.enriched_title: Acceptance probability rises with answer count and logistic trend

enriched_metadata.axes: x-axis: Number of answers; y-axis: Average Acceptance Probability

element_b.enriched_content: Black scatter points give average acceptance probability versus number of answers, increasing from roughly 0.30–0.40 at very low counts to about 0.50 by ~5,000 and then clustering around ~0.60–0.70 from ~10,000 up to ~30,000. A dashed logistic-fit curve increases monotonically, reaching ~0.80 near ~15,000 and approaching ~0.95 by ~30,000. The fitted curve lies above most observations beyond ~12,000 answers, indicating the aggregate logistic trend predicts higher acceptance than the central tendency of the later-count data. Overall, the aggregated relationship suggests increasing acceptance with more answers, while the dispersion and mid-to-high-count plateau hint at heterogeneity consistent with Simpson’s-paradox-style aggregation effects.

variables.f: target classifier whose fairness (risk difference) is being bounded
variables.h: reference/learned classifier evaluated by the surrogate fairness metric
variables.RD(f): true risk-difference (fairness disparity) of classifier f
variables.RD^+: best/optimal achievable (positive-side) risk-difference benchmark for the true metric

element_a.enriched_content: The inequality provides a lower bound on the true fairness disparity (risk difference) of a classifier f in terms of how well another classifier h performs under a δ-smoothed (surrogate) version of the same fairness measure. The term (RD_δ^+ − RD_δ(h)) is the surrogate suboptimality gap for h, and applying the inverse function ψ_δ^{-1} converts that surrogate gap into a corresponding worst-case loss in the true metric. Subtracting this converted gap from the best achievable true benchmark RD^+ yields a guaranteed lower bound on RD(f), supporting the paper’s goal of certifying fairness without explicitly adding fairness constraints during training.

element_b.enriched_content: A black 0–1 reference curve forms a step-like shape: flat near 0 for negative inputs, jumping at 0 and saturating near 1 for positive inputs. Three kappa surrogates (hinge, logistic, square) rise with the input and differ in curvature: the square kappa increases fastest for positive inputs (reaching above 2 by around x=1), hinge is piecewise-linear, and logistic increases smoothly and more gradually. Three delta surrogates (hinge, logistic, square) start negative for sufficiently negative inputs and increase toward positive values, with the hinge delta appearing roughly linear in x while logistic and square provide smoother, curved alternatives. Overall, the families provide convex, continuous approximations that bound or relax the discontinuous 0–1 indicator behavior used in risk-difference constraints.

element_a.enriched_content: The inequality provides a lower bound on the true fairness disparity (risk difference) of a classifier f in terms of how well another classifier h performs under a δ-smoothed (surrogate) version of the same fairness measure. The term (RD_δ^+ − RD_δ(h)) is the surrogate suboptimality gap for h, and applying the inverse function ψ_δ^{-1} converts that surrogate gap into a corresponding worst-case loss in the true metric. Subtracting this converted gap from the best achievable true benchmark RD^+ yields a guaranteed lower bound on RD(f), supporting the paper’s goal of certifying fairness without explicitly adding fairness constraints during training.

Three kappa surrogates (hinge, logistic, square) rise with the input and differ in curvature: the square kappa increases fastest for positive inputs (reaching above 2 by around x=1), hinge is piecewise-linear, and logistic increases smoothly and more gradually. element_a.enriched_content: Binned clutter levels are compared between ILSVRC single-object localization (dark green) and PASCAL VOC 2012 (light blue) as normalized bar heights. Both datasets concentrate at moderate clutter, with prominent peaks around clutter ≈5 (about 0.45 for ILSVRC and about 0.55 for PASCAL) and secondary mass near ≈7 (about 0.33 for ILSVRC and about 0.40 for PASCAL). ILSVRC additionally has a noticeable bar near ≈2 (~0.18) that is much smaller or absent for PASCAL, while both show very small proportions at the highest clutter bin near ≈9 (~0.05). Overall, PASCAL skews toward slightly higher clutter than ILSVRC in the dominant mid-to-high bins.

node_group.enriched_content: Binned clutter levels are compared between ILSVRC single-object localization (dark green) and PASCAL VOC 2012 (light blue) as normalized bar heights. Both datasets concentrate at moderate clutter, with prominent peaks around clutter ≈5 (about 0.45 for ILSVRC and about 0.55 for PASCAL) and secondary mass near ≈7 (about 0.33 for ILSVRC and about 0.40 for PASCAL). ILSVRC additionally has a noticeable bar near ≈2 (~0.18) that is much smaller or absent for PASCAL, while both show very small proportions at the highest clutter bin near ≈9 (~0.05). Overall, PASCAL skews toward slightly higher clutter than ILSVRC in the dominant mid-to-high bins.

element_a.enriched_content: Eight density subplots compare original predictions to counterfactual predictions after swapping a protected attribute (black↔white, asian↔white, mexican↔white, female↔male), with results shown for a “Full” model (top row) versus an “Unaware” model (bottom row). In the Full model, race swaps yield strongly separated distributions: the counterfactual curve peaks noticeably left of the original curve (lower predicted FYA), while the original curve peaks to the right (higher predicted FYA), indicating large prediction changes under racial attribute changes. In the Unaware model, the original and counterfactual curves for the race swaps nearly overlap with similar peaks and spread, indicating much smaller sensitivity of predicted FYA to the counterfactual attribute change. For the female↔male swap, the two curves remain tightly overlapping in both rows, suggesting comparatively minimal effect of changing sex on the predicted FYA distribution in this visualization.

element_a.enriched_content: The equation block defines a generative causal model where the treatment A is Bernoulli with probability pi, and the other variables are produced by linear structural equations with additive noise. element_a.enriched_content: This expression computes a marginal (interventional/counterfactual) distribution of the outcome Y by integrating over covariates C, mediator M, and intermediate variable L. The term p(Y|a,C,M,L) models the outcome given treatment and upstream variables, while p(L|a',C,M) and p(M|a,C) specify how L and M are generated under different treatment levels (a' for L, a for M), with p(C) providing the baseline distribution of confounders. Together, these factors form a g-computation formula used to identify a path-specific or mediated effect by stitching together conditional models and then marginalizing over unobserved/latent components along the causal graph.

element_a.enriched_title: Accuracy–fairness efficient frontier curves for sentencing regression models

enriched_metadata.axes: x-axis: Fairness Loss (0 to ~0.07); y-axis: Mean Squared Error (MSE, ~0.90 to ~1.02).

element_a.enriched_content: Four efficient-frontier curves trace the tradeoff between minimizing fairness loss and minimizing prediction error (MSE). As fairness loss increases from 0 toward ~0.07, MSE decreases from about 1.0 down to roughly 0.905–0.91, with the steepest improvement occurring at very small fairness loss. The group-based approaches cluster near very low fairness loss (≈0–0.01) with MSE around 0.91–0.92, while the individual-fairness curves extend across the full fairness-loss range and generally achieve slightly lower MSE at moderate-to-high fairness loss. Overall, relaxing fairness constraints yields diminishing returns in MSE reduction after about 0.03–0.05 fairness loss.

Male pronouns dominate most categories and rise from roughly the mid-30% range in Healthcare/Production to about 55–60% in STEM and Legal, indicating stronger male defaults in those fields. Neutral pronouns contribute a substantial minority (often around a quarter to a third), while female pronouns are generally smaller and vary by category, appearing relatively higher in Education and lower in STEM/Legal. The stacks visually fall slightly short of a full 100% in multiple categories, consistent with some translations not mapping cleanly to these three pronoun classes.

enriched_metadata.axes: x-axis: WEAT effect size (approximately -2 to 2); y-axis: perturbation sets labeled as increase/decrease with removal size plus baseline-0

element_a.enriched_content: Perturbation conditions (decrease-10000 through increase-10000) align along a monotonic gradient in WEAT effect size: large decreases push the effect size strongly negative (around -1.5), while large increases push it strongly positive (approaching ~1.9). Blue approximation points closely track red ground-truth points within each perturbation row, with diamond markers indicating similar per-row means for the two methods. The baseline condition clusters near a positive effect size (~1.3), and a vertical dotted reference line near that value provides a visual anchor for comparing shifts induced by removals. Agreement between approximation and ground truth remains tight across the full range, with only small offsets at some extreme perturbation sizes.

element_a.enriched_title: Reconstruction loss expansion using trace and spectral weights

variables.AP*: rank-d reconstruction of A produced by applying P*
variables.P*: learned/optimal projection (often spectral) used for reconstruction
variables.widehat{A}: best rank-d approximation of A (benchmark optimum)
variables.lambda_i*: spectral/projection coefficient associated with direction u_i
variables.u_i: orthonormal eigenvector direction used to decompose the loss
variables.Tr(·): trace operator converting quadratic forms to scalar sums
variables.||·||_F: Frobenius norm measuring squared reconstruction error

element_a.enriched_content: The formula defines a reconstruction loss as the squared Frobenius error of a chosen rank-d reconstruction AP* relative to A, measured in excess over the irreducible error achieved by the optimal rank-d approximation widehat{A}. It rewrites this excess error using trace identities to separate a constant baseline (||widehat{A}||_F^2) from terms depending on how P* aligns with the data covariance A^T A. The final expression decomposes the loss into a sum over eigen-directions u_i, where weights (2 lambda_i* − lambda_i*^2) determine how much each direction contributes, linking the loss to the paper’s spectral/projection-based reconstruction method.

element_b.enriched_title: PCA reconstruction error decreases with features, differing by gender on LFW

enriched_metadata.axes: x-axis: Number of features (principal components, ~1–20); y-axis: Reconstruction error (~10–35)

element_b.enriched_content: Reconstruction error drops steeply as the number of PCA features increases from about 1 to 5, then decreases more gradually through 20 features. The female curve remains consistently above the male curve across all feature counts, indicating higher average reconstruction error for women at the same dimensionality. At very low dimensionality the gap is largest (around mid-30s vs low-30s at ~1 feature), narrowing by 20 features where errors approach ~12 (female) and ~11 (male). The persistent separation suggests a systematic difference in how well a shared PCA representation reconstructs faces across genders.

element_a.enriched_content: The formula defines a reconstruction loss as the squared Frobenius error of a chosen rank-d reconstruction AP* relative to A, measured in excess over the irreducible error achieved by the optimal rank-d approximation widehat{A}. It rewrites this excess error using trace identities to separate a constant baseline (||widehat{A}||_F^2) from terms depending on how P* aligns with the data covariance A^T A. The final expression decomposes the loss into a sum over eigen-directions u_i, where weights (2 lambda_i* − lambda_i*^2) determine how much each direction contributes, linking the loss to the paper’s spectral/projection-based reconstruction method.

element_a.enriched_content: This formula computes the reconstruction error between an original matrix Y and its approximation Z as the sum of squared elementwise differences. The Frobenius norm aggregates deviations across all entries, and squaring yields a nonnegative loss that penalizes large discrepancies more strongly. In the paper’s context (e.g., PCA projections), this serves as the quantitative measure of how much information is lost when data are projected into a low-dimensional space and then reconstructed, enabling comparisons of average error across groups.

element_a.enriched_content: The display upper-bounds the expected distance between an input point x and an output y drawn from a distance-decaying distribution E(x). It converts the expectation into an integral over radii r, where the factor r e^{-r} weights larger radii less and |B(x,r)| captures how many points lie within distance r of x; dropping 1/Z_x uses the fact that Z_x ≥ 1. A ball-growth assumption (|B(x,r)| ≤ r^{k'}·E_x|B(x,1)|) then yields an integral of r^{k'+1}e^{-r}, giving a factorial-type bound (≈(k'+2)!) up to a 2^{O(k)} factor. This provides a dimension-dependent guarantee that the mechanism’s average distortion remains controlled when neighborhoods do not grow too quickly.

variables.P(·): probability distribution over model outputs and variables

element_a.enriched_content: The equation states that once the non-sensitive features \(\mathbf{x}\) are known, the model’s predicted outcome \(\hat{y}\) should not depend on the sensitive attribute \(z\). In the paper’s discussion of disparate mistreatment, this kind of conditional-independence criterion is used to formalize when a classifier is (or is not) using protected information beyond what is already contained in the allowed features.

element_a.enriched_content: Two stacked panels compare multiple colored point estimates with horizontal uncertainty bars for average odds difference, with most methods producing negative values between about −0.22 and 0.00. element_a.enriched_title: Fairness–performance trade-offs across bias mitigation methods using average odds difference

enriched_metadata.axes: X-axis: Average odds difference (fairness; values nearer 0 indicate better parity). Y-axis: performance metric on a 0.60–0.80 scale (exact label not visible).

element_a.enriched_content: Two stacked panels compare multiple colored point estimates with horizontal uncertainty bars for average odds difference, with most methods producing negative values between about −0.22 and 0.00. Points associated with disparate impact removal cluster around roughly −0.20 with performance near 0.74–0.75, indicating persistent negative average odds differences despite similar performance. Calibrated equal-odds postprocessing includes points much closer to 0 (around −0.02 to +0.10) while maintaining performance in the ~0.70–0.76 range, suggesting improved parity with modest performance variation. A notable outlier appears near −0.10 average odds difference with lower performance around 0.66, highlighting a potential fairness–performance trade-off for at least one setting.

element_a.enriched_title: Fair correlation bounds between culture and test score vs validity

enriched_metadata.axes: x-axis: r_XY (correlation between test score X and ground truth Y, from 0 to 1); y-axis: r_CX (correlation between culture/demographic C and test score X, from 0 to 1)

element_a.enriched_content: Four labeled relations (1–4) map permissible or “fair” values of r_CX as a function of r_XY under a fixed demographic–target correlation (stated as 0.2). Curve (1) decreases monotonically: r_CX is high when r_XY is low and approaches 0 as r_XY approaches 1, indicating diminishing allowable correlation between culture and the test as validity increases. Lines (2)–(4) are straight rays from the origin or near the baseline that meet at the rightmost point near (r_XY=1, r_CX≈0), spanning increasingly strict constraints as indicated by their vertical separation. Overall, the envelope formed by these lines/curve partitions the (r_XY, r_CX) plane into regions corresponding to Darlington’s four definitions, with stronger test validity generally implying lower acceptable culture–test correlation.

element_a.enriched_content: This objective computes a variational free energy used to fit a latent-variable generative model by optimizing both the model parameters and an approximate posterior over latent variables. The first expectation penalizes complex or unlikely explanations by measuring the negative entropy (or self-information) of the variational posterior q(H|V). The second expectation rewards settings of \theta,\phi that assign high joint probability to the observed data and inferred latents under p(V,H). In the paper’s method, introducing an explicit latent variable (e.g., H_m) makes this objective the criterion for learning the generative causal model while inferring the added latent factors.

element_a.enriched_content: Two time-series lines track daily tweet counts from 2011-12-14 through 2012-01-10, with Firehose consistently above Streaming. Firehose rises from roughly 35–45k/day in mid-December to a peak near 90k around Dec 27–28, then drops to about 27–35k/day in early January before a late spike to roughly 70k+ near Jan 10. Streaming follows a similar early level (about 30–45k/day) but undergoes a sharp drop around Dec 22 to ~8–15k/day and remains mostly below ~15k/day until a modest increase to ~25k near the end. Overall, Firehose captures substantially more tweets throughout, with the largest divergences occurring after the late-December Streaming decline and during Firehose spikes.

element_a.enriched_content: Four trajectories (labeled 0–3) separate users by how many years they survive, with longer-lived users maintaining substantially higher comments-per-submission ratios throughout tenure. The 3-year survivors rise from roughly 10–12 at start to about 17–19 by ~2 years and then plateau near that level through ~3+ years. The 2-year survivors stay near ~8–10 early and drift slightly downward after ~2 years, while 1-year survivors peak around ~9–10 near ~1–1.5 years before dropping sharply toward ~3–5 by ~2 years. The 0-year group remains lowest, hovering around ~3–5 and tapering off by about 1 year.

element_a.enriched_title: Risk minimization objective for predicting Y with surrogate output

variables.\\widetilde{Y}: chosen predictor or (possibly randomized) predicted outcome to be optimized
variables.Y: true outcome/label
variables.\\ell(\\widetilde{Y}, Y): loss function measuring prediction error or misclassification cost
variables.\\mathbb{E}: expectation over the data-generating distribution (and any predictor randomness)

element_a.enriched_content: The equation defines the learning objective as choosing a predictor \widetilde{Y} that minimizes the expected loss relative to the true label Y. The loss \ell quantifies how costly a particular prediction is, and the expectation averages this cost over the underlying population distribution (and any randomization in \widetilde{Y}). In the surrounding fairness discussion, this objective represents the utility/accuracy criterion that may be optimized subject to, or in trade-off with, constraints like equalized odds that are controlled via group-specific threshold choices on ROC curves.

element_a.enriched_title: Equalized-odds constraint matching groupwise ROC operating points

variables.a: protected-group indicator taking values 0 or 1
variables.gamma_a(\\widetilde{Y}): the (FPR, TPR) operating point achieved by the group-a predictor \widetilde{Y}
variables.\\widetilde{Y}: post-processed (possibly randomized) predictor whose rates are evaluated
variables.P_a(\\widehat{Y}): set of achievable (FPR, TPR) points for group a induced by thresholding/post-processing the base scores \widehat{Y}
variables.\\widehat{Y}: base classifier score/prediction before fairness post-processing

element_a.enriched_content: This constraint enforces that, for each protected group a, the post-processed predictor \widetilde{Y} must operate at a point on that group’s feasible ROC region derived from the base predictor \widehat{Y}. The term gamma_a(\widetilde{Y}) represents the false- and true-positive rates achieved within group a, while P_a(\widehat{Y}) encodes the set of rate pairs attainable by choosing thresholds (and possibly randomizing) applied to \widehat{Y} for that group. By requiring membership for both a=0 and a=1, the paper can select group-specific thresholds so the resulting classifier satisfies equalized-odds-style alignment of error rates across groups.

element_a.enriched_content: The equation provides an upper bound on a disparity quantity \Delta in terms of two factors: the gap between decision thresholds (t_H - t_L) and how different the two groups’ conditional distributions are, measured by total variation distance. element_a.enriched_content: This formula defines a path-specific causal effect that measures how the probability of an outcome y changes when the attribute X is switched from x1 to x2 only along selected causal pathways π. The first term computes the outcome probability under a constrained (path-specific) intervention, while the second term provides the baseline probability under the original setting. In the paper’s fairness setting, it quantifies the expected change in decisions (e.g., loan approval) for individuals from a disadvantaged group if the system were instructed to treat them as advantaged along particular mechanisms, isolating which causal routes contribute to disparity.

element_a.enriched_content: The expression defines a composite update direction for the predictor parameters that balances improving the predictor task while resisting an adversary. It starts from the predictor loss gradient, subtracts its projection onto the adversary-loss gradient so the predictor does not move in a direction that would help the adversary, and then subtracts an additional scaled adversary-gradient term to actively increase the adversary’s loss. In the method, this yields an update that preserves task learning while discouraging representations that the adversary can exploit.

element_a.caption: Figure 4: These two plots show how gender bias in coreference systems corresponds with occupational gender statistics from the U.S Bureau of Labor Statistics (left) and from text as computed by Bergsma and Lin (2006) (right); each point represents one occupation. The y-axes measure the extent to which a coref system prefers to match female pronouns with a given occupation over male pronouns, as tested by our Winogender schemas. A value of 100 (maximum female bias) means the system always resolved female pronouns to the given occupation and never male pronouns $( 1 0 0 \% - 0 \% )$ ; a score of -100 (maximum male bias) is the reverse; and a value of 0 indicates no gender differential. Recall the Winogender evaluation set is gender-balanced for each occupation; thus the horizontal dotted black line $\scriptstyle ( \mathrm { y = 0 } )$ in both plots represents a hypothetical system with $100 \%$ accuracy. Regression lines with $9 5 \%$ confidence intervals are shown.

element_a.enriched_title: Coreference gender preference correlates with occupation’s female prevalence in text

enriched_metadata.axes: x-axis: % female by occupation in text (Bergsma and Lin, 2006); y-axis: gendered pronoun resolution by occupations (%Female − %Male).

element_a.enriched_content: Three systems (STAT in blue circles, RULE in green triangles, NEURAL in red pentagons) plot occupation points against text-derived % female, with fitted trend lines and confidence bands. As the % female in text increases, all systems shift toward more female-pronoun linking (positive y), but RULE exhibits the steepest slope, reaching near +100 around 80–90% female, while STAT rises more moderately and NEURAL increases only slightly. Many occupations at low x cluster near strong male preference (around −100 to −50), and a dashed horizontal line at y=0 marks parity, which the systems cross at different x ranges (RULE earlier, STAT around mid-range, NEURAL later). The overall pattern indicates that system decisions not only track occupational gender prevalence but can amplify it, especially for the rule-based system.

element_b.caption: Table 2: System accuracy $( \% )$ bucketed by gender and difficulty (so-called “gotchas,” shaded in purple). For female pronouns, a “gotcha” sentence is one where either (1) the correct answer is OCCUPATION but the occupation is $< 5 0 \%$ female (according to BLS); or (2) the occupation is $\geq 5 0 \%$ female but the correct answer is PARTICIPANT; this is reversed for male pronouns. Systems do uniformly worse on “gotchas.”

element_a.enriched_title: Accuracy–SPD trade-off under attention-feature ablation (synthetic scenario 2)

enriched_metadata.axes: x-axis: Accuracy; y-axis: SPD (statistical parity difference)

element_a.enriched_content: A red point for the original outcome (ŷ_o) appears near Accuracy ≈ 0.62 and SPD ≈ 0.80, while several blue points (ŷ_z with specific feature indices zeroed) span markedly lower SPDs and varying accuracies. Two blue ablations at lower accuracies (≈0.50–0.54) reduce SPD to roughly ≈0.06–0.15, indicating large fairness gains accompanied by a noticeable accuracy drop. Blue points near the original accuracy (≈0.62–0.63) keep SPD high (≈0.75–0.85), implying that zeroing certain individual features does not substantially improve statistical parity at comparable predictive performance. Overall, the placements suggest a trade-off where the biggest SPD reductions occur only when accuracy decreases substantially, and near-peak accuracy models remain similarly unfair to the original.

element_b.enriched_content: This identity rewrites a centered sum of squares—total energy in the values minus the squared mean term—into an equivalent average of all pairwise squared differences among the z_i. The left-hand side computes dispersion by subtracting (1/k) times the squared sum (a mean-correction) from the sum of individual squares. The right-hand side shows the same dispersion as the average pairwise disagreement, which is useful in methods that switch between variance/centering formulations and pairwise-distance (scatter) formulations for analysis or optimization.

No specific numeric results or best-performing configuration is provided because entries are symbolic definitions rather than measured values.

element_a.enriched_content: Four efficient-frontier curves trace the tradeoff between minimizing fairness loss and minimizing prediction error (MSE). As fairness loss increases from 0 toward ~0.07, MSE decreases from about 1.0 down to roughly 0.905–0.91, with the steepest improvement occurring at very small fairness loss. The group-based approaches cluster near very low fairness loss (≈0–0.01) with MSE around 0.91–0.92, while the individual-fairness curves extend across the full fairness-loss range and generally achieve slightly lower MSE at moderate-to-high fairness loss. Overall, relaxing fairness constraints yields diminishing returns in MSE reduction after about 0.03–0.05 fairness loss.

element_a.enriched_title: Variational free-energy objective for latent-variable causal model

variables.\\mathcal{F}_{\\theta,\\phi}: training objective (free energy) depending on model and inference parameters
variables.\\theta: parameters of the generative/joint model p
variables.\\phi: parameters of the inference/sampling map f_\phi (and induced q over H)
variables.\\mathcal{E}: auxiliary noise used for reparameterized sampling
variables.f_{\\phi}(\\mathcal{E}): deterministic transform producing a sample of H from noise
variables.q_{\\epsilon}: base/noise distribution over \mathcal{E} used to define the expectation
variables.q(H): variational distribution (approximate posterior) over H induced/used by the method
variables.p(V,H): joint likelihood/prior model over observed V and latent H

element_a.enriched_content: This equation defines an objective that averages (over noise-driven samples) how well a latent-variable model explains the observed data while accounting for the variational distribution used to generate latent samples. The log p(V,H) term rewards settings of parameters that make the observed variables V and sampled latents H jointly probable under the generative/causal model, while the log q(H) term contributes the variational component that controls the complexity/entropy of the latent representation. The leading negative sign turns this expectation into a quantity to minimize, corresponding to minimizing a variational free-energy (equivalently, maximizing an ELBO-like criterion) using reparameterized samples H=f_\phi(\mathcal{E}).

element_a.enriched_title: Lagrangian objective for constrained label inference with dual variables

variables.L(λ,{y^i}): Lagrangian objective combining model scores and constraint penalties
variables.λ_j: Lagrange multiplier (dual variable) for constraint j
variables.y^i: decision variable for instance i (e.g., inferred label/assignment vector)
variables.f_θ(y^i): model scoring function parameterized by θ for assignment y^i
variables.θ: parameters of the scoring model (e.g., neural network weights)
variables.A_j: constraint coefficient/operator for constraint j applied to aggregated assignments

element_a.enriched_content: This equation defines a Lagrangian that scores a set of per-instance label/assignment variables while enforcing global linear constraints on their aggregate. The first summation adds the model’s predicted compatibility or utility f_θ for each individual assignment, encouraging choices that fit the learned model. The second term subtracts penalties weighted by λ_j for violating each constraint of the form A_j(∑_i y^i) = b_j (or ≤ b_j depending on the setup), coupling all instances through a dataset-level condition. In the paper’s method, this Lagrangian enables constrained inference or learning by alternating between optimizing the assignments y^i and updating the dual variables λ to satisfy the constraints.

element_a.enriched_content: The expression defines a composite update direction for the predictor parameters that balances improving the predictor task while resisting an adversary. It starts from the predictor loss gradient, subtracts its projection onto the adversary-loss gradient so the predictor does not move in a direction that would help the adversary, and then subtracts an additional scaled adversary-gradient term to actively increase the adversary’s loss. In the method, this yields an update that preserves task learning while discouraging representations that the adversary can exploit.

element_b.enriched_title: Decomposition of centered sum of squares into pairwise differences

variables.z_i: scalar value for index i (e.g., sample/feature/component)
variables.j: second index for pairs of elements
variables.m: upper limit of the inner sum (likely intended to equal k)

element_b.enriched_content: This identity rewrites a centered sum of squares—total energy in the values minus the squared mean term—into an equivalent average of all pairwise squared differences among the z_i. The left-hand side computes dispersion by subtracting (1/k) times the squared sum (a mean-correction) from the sum of individual squares. The right-hand side shows the same dispersion as the average pairwise disagreement, which is useful in methods that switch between variance/centering formulations and pairwise-distance (scatter) formulations for analysis or optimization.

element_a.enriched_title: Projected adversarial-gradient update direction for predictor weights

variables.∇_W L_P: gradient of predictor loss w.r.t. W
variables.∇_W L_A: gradient of adversary loss w.r.t. W
variables.proj_{∇_W L_A}(∇_W L_P): component of the predictor gradient aligned with the adversary gradient direction
variables.α: scalar weight controlling strength of adversarial term

element_a.enriched_content: The expression defines a composite update direction for the predictor parameters that balances improving the predictor task while resisting an adversary. It starts from the predictor loss gradient, subtracts its projection onto the adversary-loss gradient so the predictor does not move in a direction that would help the adversary, and then subtracts an additional scaled adversary-gradient term to actively increase the adversary’s loss. In the method, this yields an update that preserves task learning while discouraging representations that the adversary can exploit.

element_a.enriched_title: Variational free-energy objective for latent-variable causal model

variables.\\mathcal{F}_{\\theta,\\phi}: training objective (free energy) depending on model and inference parameters
variables.\\theta: parameters of the generative/joint model p
variables.\\phi: parameters of the inference/sampling map f_\phi (and induced q over H)
variables.\\mathcal{E}: auxiliary noise used for reparameterized sampling
variables.f_{\\phi}(\\mathcal{E}): deterministic transform producing a sample of H from noise
variables.q_{\\epsilon}: base/noise distribution over \mathcal{E} used to define the expectation
variables.q(H): variational distribution (approximate posterior) over H induced/used by the method
variables.p(V,H): joint likelihood/prior model over observed V and latent H

element_a.enriched_content: This equation defines an objective that averages (over noise-driven samples) how well a latent-variable model explains the observed data while accounting for the variational distribution used to generate latent samples. The log p(V,H) term rewards settings of parameters that make the observed variables V and sampled latents H jointly probable under the generative/causal model, while the log q(H) term contributes the variational component that controls the complexity/entropy of the latent representation. The leading negative sign turns this expectation into a quantity to minimize, corresponding to minimizing a variational free-energy (equivalently, maximizing an ELBO-like criterion) using reparameterized samples H=f_\phi(\mathcal{E}).

element_a.enriched_title: Lagrangian objective for constrained label inference with dual variables

variables.L(λ,{y^i}): Lagrangian objective combining model scores and constraint penalties
variables.λ_j: Lagrange multiplier (dual variable) for constraint j
variables.y^i: decision variable for instance i (e.g., inferred label/assignment vector)
variables.f_θ(y^i): model scoring function parameterized by θ for assignment y^i
variables.θ: parameters of the scoring model (e.g., neural network weights)
variables.A_j: constraint coefficient/operator for constraint j applied to aggregated assignments

element_a.enriched_content: This equation defines a Lagrangian that scores a set of per-instance label/assignment variables while enforcing global linear constraints on their aggregate. The first summation adds the model’s predicted compatibility or utility f_θ for each individual assignment, encouraging choices that fit the learned model. The second term subtracts penalties weighted by λ_j for violating each constraint of the form A_j(∑_i y^i) = b_j (or ≤ b_j depending on the setup), coupling all instances through a dataset-level condition. In the paper’s method, this Lagrangian enables constrained inference or learning by alternating between optimizing the assignments y^i and updating the dual variables λ to satisfy the constraints.

enriched_metadata.axes: x-axis: training gender ratio (0 to 1); y-axis: predicted gender ratio (about -0.2 to 1.2)

element_b.enriched_content: Red scatter points map individual categories’ predicted gender ratios against their training gender ratios, forming a strong positive association across the 0–1 range. A solid diagonal reference line and two dashed bounds bracket the main trend, while a fitted line closely tracks the diagonal, indicating predictions generally follow training prevalence but with noticeable dispersion. Many points deviate substantially (often by ~0.1–0.3 in ratio), including outliers where predictions are much higher or lower than what training data suggests. The overall pattern indicates prediction behavior is strongly tied to training gender imbalance, consistent with bias propagation when RBA is not applied.

element_a.enriched_title: Derivative of conditional acceptance probability at a reference point

variables.X_c: child/outcome random variable (e.g., acceptance or class indicator)
variables.X_p: parent/conditioning random variable (e.g., user activity or feature)
variables.a: reference value for the outcome and conditioning variable
variables.x_p: value of the conditioning variable at which the conditional probability is evaluated
variables.d/dx_p: derivative measuring local sensitivity to changes in x_p

element_a.enriched_content: The equation states that the local rate of change of the conditional probability that the outcome equals a, as the conditioning variable x_p changes, is evaluated at x_p=a and equals the negative of that same conditional probability at x_p=a. The left-hand side measures sensitivity: how quickly the chance of X_c=a changes with small increases in X_p near a. The right-hand side imposes a specific decreasing relationship, meaning higher X_p near a reduces the probability at a in direct proportion to its current level. In the paper’s context, this supports the claim that, holding other factors fixed (e.g., reputation), greater activity (more answers) does not increase—and may decrease—the probability of a new answer being accepted.

enriched_metadata.axes: Rows correspond to user groups; columns correspond to movie genres/items (Horror, Romance, Drama).

element_a.enriched_content: Block-structured user–movie rating patterns separate “horror lovers” from “romance lovers”: one group assigns high ratings to Horror and low ratings to Romance, while the other reverses this, and both assign mid-level ratings to Drama. Propensities and the binary observation indicator concentrate observations in each group’s preferred genre, leaving systematic gaps in the cross-genre entries (a missing-not-at-random pattern). Two predicted rating matrices contrast outcomes under this biased observation process, with one aligning with the observed-selection structure and the other aiming to reconstruct the underlying block-constant ratings. An intervention indicator matrix marks a targeted subset of entries for additional observation, emphasizing the missing cross-genre ratings needed to disambiguate user preferences.

element_b.enriched_content: The equation shows that the expected value (over the observation process O) of the inverse propensity scoring (IPS) estimator of risk equals the full-data average risk R(hatY). element_b.enriched_content: This identity rewrites a centered sum of squares—total energy in the values minus the squared mean term—into an equivalent average of all pairwise squared differences among the z_i. The right-hand side shows the same dispersion as the average pairwise disagreement, which is useful in methods that switch between variance/centering formulations and pairwise-distance (scatter) formulations for analysis or optimization.

node_group.enriched_title: Decomposition of centered sum of squares into pairwise differences

variables.z_i: scalar value for index i (e.g., sample/feature/component)
variables.j: second index for pairs of elements
variables.m: upper limit of the inner sum (likely intended to equal k)

node_group.enriched_content: This identity rewrites a centered sum of squares—total energy in the values minus the squared mean term—into an equivalent average of all pairwise squared differences among the z_i. The left-hand side computes dispersion by subtracting (1/k) times the squared sum (a mean-correction) from the sum of individual squares. The right-hand side shows the same dispersion as the average pairwise disagreement, which is useful in methods that switch between variance/centering formulations and pairwise-distance (scatter) formulations for analysis or optimization.

element_b.enriched_title: Cost-sensitive empirical risk minimization classifier selection

variables.h: candidate classifier from the hypothesis class
variables.c_i^1: cost incurred if example i is predicted as class 1
variables.c_i^0: cost incurred if example i is predicted as class 0

element_b.enriched_content: This objective chooses a classifier \(\hat{h}\) from a hypothesis class \(\mathcal{H}\) that minimizes the total, per-example prediction cost over the training set. For each instance \(X_i\), predicting 1 (i.e., \(h(X_i)=1\)) contributes cost \(c_i^1\), while predicting 0 contributes cost \(c_i^0\); the expression mixes these two costs according to the model’s binary output. In the paper’s method, this serves as the core cost-sensitive learning rule, allowing different examples (and potentially different groups) to impose different penalties for the two possible predictions.

variables.K: random variable modeled as Gaussian noise/latent factor

element_a.enriched_content: This statement specifies that the variable K is modeled as a standard normal random variable, meaning it has zero mean and unit variance. The mean 0 centers K so it introduces no systematic bias, while the variance 1 fixes the scale of its randomness. In the paper’s linear-model context, this kind of assumption typically provides a simple, well-calibrated noise or latent input that can be used to analyze properties of the predictor (e.g., whether predictions are unaffected by a sensitive attribute).

element_a.enriched_title: Class-conditional Gaussian model for features given group and label

variables.mu: mean vector of the conditional feature distribution
variables.Sigma: covariance matrix of the conditional feature distribution

element_a.enriched_content: This equation specifies the generative data distribution for the feature vector x when the sensitive attribute is z = 1 and the label is y = −1. Under this condition, x is modeled as a multivariate Gaussian with mean vector [−5, 0], which sets the expected location of points, and covariance matrix [[5, 1], [1, 5]], which controls the spread of the data and the correlation between the two feature dimensions. In the paper’s scenario, such group- and label-conditional distributions define the synthetic populations used to visualize decision boundaries and analyze accuracy–fairness trade-offs.

element_a.enriched_title: Conditional independence of prediction from sensitive attribute given features

variables.P(·): probability distribution over model outputs and variables
variables.\\mathbf{x}: observed non-sensitive feature vector used for prediction

element_a.enriched_content: The equation states that once the non-sensitive features \(\mathbf{x}\) are known, the model’s predicted outcome \(\hat{y}\) should not depend on the sensitive attribute \(z\). The left-hand side is the distribution of predictions conditioned on both \(\mathbf{x}\) and \(z\), while the right-hand side is the distribution conditioned only on \(\mathbf{x}\); setting them equal encodes a fairness requirement. In the paper’s discussion of disparate mistreatment, this kind of conditional-independence criterion is used to formalize when a classifier is (or is not) using protected information beyond what is already contained in the allowed features.

In the paper’s discussion of disparate mistreatment, this kind of conditional-independence criterion is used to formalize when a classifier is (or is not) using protected information beyond what is already contained in the allowed features.

element_b.enriched_content: This equation defines a binary classifier that outputs 1 when a continuous score R exceeds a threshold and 0 otherwise. The indicator function converts the score comparison into a hard decision, while the threshold T_a can vary by group a to tune group-conditional true/false positive rates. In the paper’s equalized-odds setting, choosing different T_a values corresponds to selecting points on each group’s ROC curve and finding feasible intersections that satisfy fairness constraints.

element_b.enriched_title: Fairlet decomposition runtime scales with sample size on Census II

enriched_metadata.axes: x-axis: Number of sub-sampled points (0 to ~2,500,000); y-axis: Runtime in seconds (0 to ~400).

element_b.enriched_content: Runtime increases roughly monotonically as the number of sub-sampled points grows, indicating near-linear scaling over most of the range. The curve rises from about 10–20 seconds at ~100k points to ~150 seconds near 1.1M, ~210 seconds around 1.5M, and ~290–300 seconds at ~2.1M. A local peak occurs near ~2.35M points at roughly 360 seconds, followed by a slight drop to about 350 seconds by ~2.4M. Overall, larger samples substantially increase computation time for the (1,2)-fairlet decomposition on Census II.

element_b.enriched_title: Stereotypical analogies versus generated analogies under debiasing methods

enriched_metadata.axes: x-axis: number of generated analogies; y-axis: number of stereotypic analogies

element_b.enriched_content: As the number of generated analogies increases (0–160), the count of stereotypic analogies rises for the original embedding (“before”) from ~0 up to about 29. Soft-debiased embeddings reduce this growth modestly, ending around ~25 stereotypic analogies at the highest generation counts, with a similar upward trend after ~70–80 analogies. Hard-debiased embeddings suppress stereotypic analogies much more strongly, staying near 0 until roughly ~60 analogies and remaining below ~10 even at ~150 generated analogies. Overall, hard debiasing produces the largest reduction in stereotypical analogies relative to both the baseline and soft debiasing.
